messages.subject: Using hcov in secr.fit for polygon data causes R session abort
messages.subject_clean: Using hcov in secr.fit for polygon data causes R session abort
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am new to secr and would like to fit a hybrid mixture model to account for sex differences in my polygon data (pine marten faecal samples collected within a study area, single search).
When I include the term hcov = "sex" in secr.fit, it almost immediately terminates my complete R session saying "R Session Aborted - R encountered fatal error" (R version 4.1.3). I get no helpful error messages to do some troubleshooting.

I tried to run the model on two different mashines with the same result (operating systems windows 10 22H2 and ubuntu 22.04).
Further I tried to fit a hybrid mixture model with the polygon example data polygonCH ( I added the covariate sex with randomly created "f" and "m" as factors for each detected animal) to check whether my pine marten capthist data might be prepared wrong but again the R session terminates. However, running the example data from ?hcov for the housemouse trap data works perfectly fine.

Did anyone encounter this problem before?
Is it not possible to include hcov in polygon data?

Any help would be much appreciated!

Thanks,
Henriette

My reply contained an error, as can be seen from the actual example further down. It should have read -
for (i in 1:7) timevaryingcov(traps(secr_data_dups[[i]])) <- list(type = 1:9)

This allows 'type' to be used in model formulae (I checked). You will get into trouble using numeric codes for trap types (0,1,2,3 implies ascending numeric values). Character values will be treated automatically as factor levels, which is what you intend. (Incidentally, please format your code so it is readable; use spaces, indent, omit unnecessary arguments etc.).

On Friday, 26 May 2023 at 23:31:21 UTC+3 murray...@gmail.com wrote:
> 'binary.usage' is an argument of read.traps that has no downstream effect, as I remember. Once upon a time, all 'usage' data were binary, then the capability expanded (the code in read.traps from 2012 is still marked as 'tentative'!). 'binary.usage' merely switches between old and new input code blocks. The usage matrix of a traps object can mix binary and non-binary.
>
> So I suggest you simply enter the trap- and occasion-specific values together with binary.usage = FALSE. Use only spaces, not commas (until a fix I have just applied on GitHub percolates through to another CRAN version of secr).
>
> Of course, you will need to model differing detection parameters.
>
> Murray
>
> On Saturday, May 27, 2023 at 2:50:43 AM UTC+12 charlott...@gmail.com wrote:
> > Hi everyone,
> >
> > I’m carrying out an analysis of lion density using two data sets: camera trap data from a camera trap survey, and direct sightings data from a search-encounter survey. Both the surveys were carried out in the same area and during the same period.
> >
> > In addition to comparing the separate density estimates produced through these two survey types, I'd like to try and combine the different data types into a single model. This is because I expect it should improve my density estimate (by virtue of increasing the number of captures and recaptures), and more broadly because I think it could be a useful approach in certain contexts, and would like to work out how (if!) it can be done.
> >
> > I’ve already modelled both these datasets separately in secr. For the camera trap data, I used proximity detectors with binary effort. For the search encounter data, I converted the study area into a 1x1km grid of cells, with effort calculated as the number of kilometres driven in that cell on that day – this means it is also proximity detector type, but with a different (non-binary) measure of effort.
> >
> > I know that there is currently no function to pool capthist data from different detector arrays, and that it is recommended to merge the input files and rebuild the capthist object from scratch. However, is it possible to do this with two different survey methods with different measures of effort (binary and non-binary)?
> >
> > Otherwise it would be possible to use a binary measure of effort for the search encounter data (i.e. 1 if that pixel was surveyed on that sampling occasion, 0 if it was not) and combine it with the camera trap data into a single set of input files. However, the actual effort is really quite different between the two data types, so this seems like it may not be a good way forward.
> >
> > Any advice would be much appreciated!
> >
> > Thanks,
> > Charlotte

messages.body_plain:
There is indeed a bug that causes secr.fit to crash when faced with polygon data and hcov. I have fixed it for the next release, but that is a few weeks away. Meantime, I suggest you think about discretizing polygon detectors: it's much faster, and the code for point (e.g., 'proximity') detectors is more stable and better tested. Compare, for example,

# 600 seconds
# after fixing 'hcov' bug
fit_hcov = secr.fit(polygonCH, buffer = 200, hcov = "value", trace = TRUE)
coef(fit_hcov)
#                 beta    SE.beta        lcl       ucl
# D         0.09845739 0.13858501 -0.1731642 0.3700790
# lambda0   1.47621420 0.09548916  1.2890589 1.6633695
# sigma     3.90088946 0.04914132  3.8045742 3.9972047
# pmix.h2m -0.03636427 0.26972486 -0.5650153 0.4922867

# 25 seconds
CH <- discretize(polygonCH, spacing = 25)
fit_hcov_discretized <- secr.fit(CH, buffer = 200, hcov = "value", trace = TRUE)
coef(fit_hcov_discretized)
#                 beta    SE.beta        lcl        ucl
# D         0.09234172 0.13872995 -0.1795640  0.3642474
# lambda0  -1.70417134 0.12836875 -1.9557695 -1.4525732

messages.body_plain:
The format for effort codes was designed originally to allow a string of zeros and ones e.g. 011011. Obviously that wasn't going to work for non-binary effort, so space-separated fields were allowed. More recently, csv input has become common so the format needed to catch up. I don't know right off whether commas are a problem elsewhere, but if you don't need csv it probably is safer to avoid them.
Murray

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone, I am currently comparing the density patterns of two lemurs across two forest landscapes. My models include a habitat mask with info about the distance to the forest edge. I ran models that combined the two landscapes - these models had no issues. Next, unique models for the two landscapes. The models from the first landscape were fine. Unfortunately, the models from the second landscape errored when I include the habitat mask - Warning: missing values in predictors?Error in lpred[, 1] <- Yp : replacement has length zero
Thank you for any help you may provide
--
MM.M.CAPHIST <- read.capthist(captfile = "MM_M_CapturesData.csv", trapfile = "TrapsMData.csv", detector = "multi")
summary(MM.M.CAPHIST)
M_ED <- raster("EdgeDist_M.tif")
M_TRAP_BUFFER <- traps(MM.M.CAPHIST)
M_MASK <- make.mask(M_TRAP_BUFFER, buffer = 408, spacing = 10, type = "trapbuffer")
M_MASK <- addCovariates(object = M_MASK, spatialdata = M_ED)
MM_M.SCR_ED.FIT <- secr.fit(MM.M.CAPHIST, mask = M_MASK, detectfn = 'HN', method = "Nelder-Mead", model = D ~ EdgeDist_M, trace = FALSE, ncores = 8)
MM_M.SCR_NULL.FIT <- secr.fit(MM.M.CAPHIST, buffer = 408, detectfn = 'HR', trace = FALSE)

Hello Fernando
Trying with the data you provide:
1. addCovariates clearly warns about missing values in covariates
2. secr.fit() states that these are set to zero when fitting, but predict() doesn't cope unless you provide covariate values manually, e.g.
predict(MM_M.SCR_ED.FIT, newdata=data.frame(EdgeDist_M = seq(-500,1500,500)))
3. your mask is much bigger than it needs to be (>200 000 points). I would use buffer = 100; that gives no warnings or errors.
4. your NULL.FIT model constructs a mask on the fly (64 points east-west). This is dangerous as your sampling is highly fragmented. Also, you change the detection function.
5. I would be wary of your density model. The covariate includes negative distances. Because the density link is 'log' you are fitting a log-linear model, and that predicts extremely high and extremely low densities at the extremes.
Murray

messages.body_plain:
I understand your confusion. g0 and lambda0 are intercept parameters corresponding to alternative ways of specifying the detection function, so you use one or the other. g0 is the appropriate parameter when the detection function is specified in terms of probability of detection vs distance (detectfn = 'HN', 'EX' etc.). lambda0 is the appropriate parameter when the detection function is expressed in terms of the hazard of detection vs distance (detectfn = 'HHN', 'HEX' etc.). The default detectfn is 'HN', so by default g0 is used. A detection function specified in terms of the hazard of detection has some properties that make manipulation easier (e.g. computing expected counts in secrdesign), and my intuition suggests it is closer to the corresponding home range model (e.g., circular bivariate normal = 'HHN'). But in practice no-one really minds which you use. Check ?detectfn.
